22-2.title: Ask for the price card before you order and keep the bill — an extra added at the end is the part you can actually dispute
22-2.cost: No cost. Ask for the price list before ordering, and keep the bill.
22-2.inPlainWords: There is no single central rule that makes every restaurant or venue in India display its prices. Packaged goods are the part the law covers clearly: the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011 require the retail sale price, the quantity and the manufacturer's details to be printed on the pack, and a shop may not charge above that price. For a restaurant or a venue, ask for the menu or the rate card before you order, and confirm the price of anything sold by weight or at 'market rate' before it is cooked. A service charge is not compulsory: the Department of Consumer Affairs' 2022 guidelines say it may not be levied automatically, and you can ask for it to be removed. A false or misleading price is an unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019; keep the bill and complain to the National Consumer Helpline on 1915.
22-2.benefit: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 covers a false or misleading price and a deficient service, and a complaint can go to the district consumer commission for a refund and compensation. The bill should show the tax and the total. For a packaged item the printed retail sale price is the ceiling. For a restaurant, the practical protection is the price you were shown plus the bill: ask what the 'market price' dish costs before it is cooked, and ask for the service charge to be taken off if you do not want to pay it.
22-2.caveats: A 'market price' item should be quoted before cooking. A service charge is not a tip and is not compulsory: the 2022 guidelines say it must not be levied automatically, so ask for it to be removed. A venue's 'minimum charge' should be shown before you sit down.
22-2.sources: Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Department of Consumer Affairs, guidelines on service charge. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; National Consumer Helpline. <https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/>

22-1.title: Check where the emergency exits are before you enter a bar, a club or an escape room; if they are locked or blocked, pick another venue
22-1.cost: No cost at all. Ten seconds looking around as you walk in.
22-1.inPlainWords: India has no single national law that spells out exit rules for every bar, club or escape room: fire safety is a state subject, and a venue is licensed and inspected under the state fire rules, the municipal by-laws and, for a large building, the National Building Code of India 2016. What that means in practice is simple: an exit that is locked, blocked by stacked chairs or crates, or hidden behind a curtain is a defect in the premises, and the person to tell is the local fire officer or the municipal licence department, not only the manager. If a private room is in a basement, has only one way out, or the corridor is cluttered, choose a different venue.
22-1.benefit: A licensed venue is required to keep its means of escape usable and its exit signs lit, and the state fire service issues the no-objection certificate on which the trade licence depends. The National Building Code of India 2016 sets out the exit widths, travel distances and signage a building is designed to, and states adopt it through their fire rules. A licensed place that fails an inspection can lose the licence, which is why a complaint to the fire officer carries weight. Escape rooms and clubs in converted houses are the ones most often outside that system entirely.
22-1.caveats: If any of these is present, pick another venue: a private room underground, only one exit, a corridor filled with clutter, or an exit light that is dead. In a fire at such a place, smoke, narrow corridors and a crowd that has been drinking make escape far harder than it looks from the doorway — you may have seconds. Look for the exit before you sit down, and count the doors between your seat and the street.
22-1.sources: National Building Code of India 2016, Bureau of Indian Standards. <https://www.bis.gov.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

22-3.title: If someone offers you drugs at a venue, leave — possession is an offence in India, and a room you booked is your responsibility
22-3.inPlainWords: Under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, it is an offence to produce, possess, sell, buy, transport or use a narcotic drug or a psychotropic substance, and the punishment depends on the quantity seized — small, commercial or intermediate — and on the substance. There is no separate 'public order' penalty here: even a first offence with a small quantity can mean prison, and a commercial quantity carries a much heavier sentence decided by a special court. A venue that allows drug use on its premises risks its excise and police licence. If someone offers you an unknown powder, a pill or a vape cartridge, walk away right then.
22-3.benefit: The Act classifies quantities and the sentence follows the class; consumption is dealt with separately, and abetment and conspiracy are offences in their own right, so 'I only passed it on' is not a defence. The seizing officer can arrest and the case is tried by a special court. A bar or club that breaches its licence conditions can lose its excise licence, and that is the leverage a complaint to the excise or police licensing authority uses. None of this makes the venue the judge: your own possession is the offence you carry.
22-3.caveats: If anyone offers you unknown powders, pills or vape cartridges to try, leave immediately — do not stay to watch. Individual liability is heavier than the venue's: possession is the offence, and a room you booked or a flat you share is where the search happens. 'It was not mine' is a defence that has to be proved. If a friend collapses after taking something, call 112 and stay with them; the medical emergency comes before the legal question.
22-3.sources: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Central Bureau of Narcotics. <https://cbn.nic.in/>

22-4.title: Do not accept candy or snacks from strangers, do not drink a beverage you left unattended, and do not take a vape cartridge handed to you by someone else
22-4.inPlainWords: The drugs that turn up in drinks and vapes are not the ones people picture. The reported cases involve sedatives and vape liquid spiked with a synthetic cannabinoid, and the point of spiking is robbery or assault, not a joke. Giving someone a drug without their knowledge is an offence under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, and so is possessing it; the sentence depends on the substance and the quantity and is decided by a court. There is no published fine table for drugging someone. Any drink that has been out of your sight should be replaced, not finished.
22-4.benefit: Synthetic cannabinoids are controlled as psychotropic substances under the NDPS Act, and its schedules are amended by notification as new compounds appear, so a cartridge that was not covered last year may be now. A spiked drink is usually about robbery or sexual assault: the drug makes the victim compliant and the memory unreliable, and what is lost is the phone, the cash and the account passwords. Replacing a drink is cheap; a blood or urine test after the fact is not, and it has to be done within hours to be useful.
22-4.caveats: This applies at a school gate, a friend's party and on a long-distance bus, not only at a bar, and it works the same whether the offer is candy, a drink or a vape cartridge. After being drugged, victims often lose money, a phone, or worse; no Indian statistic reliably counts it, so treat it as a warning drawn from cases rather than a rate. If you feel suddenly and inexplicably drunk, tell someone you trust and get to a hospital — a test in the first hours is the evidence. For unknown powders or cartridges found in such a setting, see item 3.
22-4.sources: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Central Bureau of Narcotics. <https://cbn.nic.in/>

22-5.title: Avoid escape rooms and scripted mystery games in residential buildings or below the first basement
22-5.inPlainWords: India has no rule aimed specifically at escape rooms or scripted mystery games. What applies is the ordinary licensing chain: a commercial entertainment premises needs a trade licence from the municipal body, a fire no-objection certificate from the state fire service, and a police licence under the state police or places-of-public-resort rules. A game run out of a flat is outside all of it. The risk is structural: a basement room with one stair, partitions that make a maze, props that burn, and doors that are meant to be opened by solving a puzzle. Before you book, ask what floor it is on and whether the building is commercial.
22-5.benefit: A fire no-objection certificate is issued against a specific premises and a specific use, and a residential flat cannot hold one for a public entertainment use; the state fire rules and the National Building Code of India 2016 set the travel distance, exit width and signage that a basement needs. A venue that cannot show a trade licence and a fire certificate is running on the assumption that nothing will go wrong. The same logic applies to a club or a banquet hall in a converted house.
22-5.caveats: These places are usually dark, cut into small rooms, full of flammable props, and the door sometimes needs a puzzle solved to open. In a fire that is far harder to escape than from an ordinary shop. You can check the floor and the building type on a review page before booking, but the licence is the real test: ask to see it, and walk away if the answer is a shrug. If the only exit you can find is the one you came in by, leave.
22-5.sources: National Building Code of India 2016, Bureau of Indian Standards. <https://www.bis.gov.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

22-11.benefit: Forensic analyses in Finland examining all sauna-related deaths from 1990 to 2002 using police and medical examiner records found that approximately 50% of decedents were under the influence of alcohol at the time of death, highlighting alcohol as the primary modifiable fatal risk factor. In Tokyo, Japan, medical examiners reviewed 3,289 sudden bath-related deaths occurring between 2009 and 2011; among 550 autopsied cases, 140 (approx. 25.5%) had blood alcohol concentrations exceeding 0.5 mg/mL. In a forensic series of 77 bathtub drowning fatalities in Tokyo, acute alcohol intoxication was identified as the leading contributing factor (25 cases), surpassing pre-existing heart disease (22 cases). The Consumer Affairs Agency of Japan reported 7,776 domestic bathtub drowning deaths in 2024 (7,363 among adults over 65), issuing explicit safety guidelines cautioning that bathing immediately after meals, alcohol intake, or sedating medication drastically elevates fatal risk. The mechanism is the same everywhere: hot water and a hot room dilate the peripheral blood vessels, blood pressure falls, and the brain is briefly under-perfused, which is why an intoxicated person can black out in a bath or on a sauna bench.
22-11.sources: Kenttämies A, Karkola K (2008). Death in sauna. Journal of Forensic Sciences, 53(3), 724-729. <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1556-4029.2008.00703.x>; Suzuki H, Hikiji W, Tanifuji T, Abe N, Fukunaga T (2015). Characteristics of sudden bath-related death investigated by medical examiners in Tokyo, Japan. Journal of Epidemiology, 25(2), 126-132. <https://doi.org/10.2188/jea.JE20140068>; Mishima S, Suzuki H, Fukunaga T, Nishitani Y (2018). Postmortem computed tomography findings in cases of bath-related death: applicability and limitation in forensic practice. Forensic Science International, 282, 195-203. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.forsciint.2017.11.030>; Consumer Affairs Agency of Japan (2025). Caution regarding elderly accidents during New Year holidays: Avoid bathing immediately after meals, drinking, or medication. <https://www.caa.go.jp/policies/policy/consumer_safety/caution/caution_084/>

22-12.cost: A certified bicycle helmet costs upwards of a thousand rupees, and a ski or snowboard helmet more; the cost of using it is five seconds to buckle it before each session.
22-12.benefit: A meta-analysis of 12 studies on skiing and snowboarding injuries found that helmet use was associated with a 35% reduction in head injuries (odds ratio OR 0.65; 95% CI 0.55–0.79). Among children under 13, the protective effect was even greater, reducing head injuries by 59% (OR 0.41; 95% CI 0.27–0.59). Helmet use did not increase neck injury risk (OR 0.89; 95% CI 0.72–1.09). For cycling, a systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 studies covering over 64,000 injured cyclists found that helmet use reduced head injury by 51% (OR 0.49; 95% CI 0.42–0.57), severe head injury by 69% (OR 0.31; 95% CI 0.25–0.37), and fatal head injury by 65% (OR 0.35; 95% CI 0.14–0.88). Facial injuries were reduced by 33% (OR 0.67; 95% CI 0.56–0.81), with no significant association with neck trauma (OR 0.96; 95% CI 0.74–1.25). No Indian law requires a helmet on a ski slope — India has very few organised ski areas and no national ski helmet rule — but the rental shop and the ski school usually require one, and the helmet protects you whatever the rule says.
22-12.sources: Russell K, Christie J, Hagel BE (2010). The effect of helmets on the risk of head and neck injuries among skiers and snowboarders: a meta-analysis. CMAJ, 182(4), 333-340. <https://doi.org/10.1503/cmaj.091080>; Olivier J, Creighton P (2017). Bicycle injuries and helmet use: a systematic review and meta-analysis. International Journal of Epidemiology, 46(1), 278-292. <https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw153>
